title: The November Collections Window: Why Debtors You Don't Chase Now Become a January Cash Problem
linkedin:
Right now, every invoice sitting in your debtors ledger looks like an ordinary unpaid invoice.

In six to eight weeks, once customers close for the Christmas break, some of those invoices become cash you genuinely can't reach. Not unpaid by choice, just out of reach, because the person who signs off payment runs is already on leave.

Here's the part that catches owners out: the real deadline falls weeks before the office actually closes.

Payment approvals slow down well before the shutdown date itself. Construction clients, professional services firms and anyone adjacent to government payment cycles often lock in their last payment run of the year by mid-to-late November. Chase an overdue invoice with these customers in December, and in practical terms you're waiting until February.

The timing lands badly for a second reason. The same weeks debtors freeze are usually the weeks your own costs peak, Christmas stock, casual wages for extended trading hours, bonuses, the usual quarterly obligations that don't pause for anyone's holiday. Cash gets trapped in the ledger exactly when you need it flowing the other way.

A business that looks perfectly healthy on paper in November can find itself genuinely short in December, purely because receivables froze while payables kept moving on schedule.

The fix starts now, not in the new year: rank debtors by age and size, chase the ones that would actually hurt if they slipped past the freeze, and progress-bill anything running into December rather than waiting for one completion invoice in mid-month.
